summary: Foster City is literally built on landfill — a planned community engineered in the 1960s from Bay mud and dredged sand on the western shore of the San Francisco Bay, which means nearly every street sits at or just above sea level, protected by a ring of levees, and many homes back onto a network of interconnected lagoons where people kayak after work. That unusual geography delivers something rare on the Peninsula: flat, open-sky water views without coastal bluffs or hillside switchbacks, plus a continuous paved loop trail around the lagoon system that connects parks, playgrounds, and shoreline paths into a single walkable circuit. The job center question is genuinely interesting here: Gilead Sciences and Visa both have major campuses in town, meaning a meaningful number of jobs exist within city limits — but with a median home value north of $1.77 million against a median household income around $194K (a price-to-income ratio above 9:1), even well-compensated households face serious arithmetic on ownership. Year-round weather barely fluctuates — average highs hover near 67°F with roughly nine hours of daily sunshine — so the lagoon trails get steady use across all seasons. Foster City is the rare Silicon Valley bedroom-community-that-isn't-quite-one: substantial employers inside its borders, but a housing cost structure that still prices in proximity to everywhere else.
